steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on t-METASET, an active learning framework for building task-aware, less biased metamaterial datasets. Cover metamaterials and data-driven design, the overlooked problem of data acquisition and property bias, the limits of METASET, our approach, contributions and how we validate it.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Metamaterials and the need for design methods
2. Data-driven metamaterials design (DDMD)
3. Neglected problem: data acquisition and data quality
4. METASET and its limitations
5. t-METASET: task-aware data acquisition
6. Contributions, advantages and validation

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Metamaterials
- artificially architectured materials; unusual properties from structure, not composition
- computing power + manufacturing -> theory, computational design, experiments
- last two decades: optical, acoustic, thermal, mechanical properties
- applications: communications, aerospace, biomedical, defense
- designability in hierarchical systems key; superior functionalities, customization, miniaturization
- growing demand for advanced design methods

2. DDMD
- three steps: data acquisition, model construction, inference for design
- precomputed dataset of many structure-property pairs
- ML learns structure -> property (sometimes reverse)
- design optimization at "building block"/unit cell level, optional macroscale tiling for aperiodic designs
- distinctions: (i) accelerates multiscale design, explores vast space; (ii) few restrictions on analytical formulations; (iii) some on-demand without iterations, pays off initial cost
- many achievements recently

3. Data acquisition neglected
- rare attention to data acquisition / quality assessment, the first step
- data is a design element; landscape learned by model ("abstraction"), explored by inference/optimization
- data quality propagates downstream; impact of naive acquisition opaque, hard to prevent a priori
- common practice: many space-filling designs in shape space -> imbalance (distributional bias) in property space
- training, validation, deployment without rigorous assessment (diversity, design quality, feasibility)
- overlooks imbalance and compounding ramification at design stage

4. METASET (Chan et al.)
- subset selection: small but diverse subsets from fully evaluated database
- evaluate all properties a priori, downsample balanced subset by diversity metrics
- limits: (i) evaluation too expensive for massive (\sim O(10^{4})) database; (ii) diversity alone no customization for tasks

5. t-METASET
- task-aware METASET; starts from sparse observations
- "task-aware": rate points by utility for a specific design scenario, not distributional metrics
- diversity (bias reduction, generic) + quality (particular use) as sampling criteria
- advocate: (i) iterative dataset building; (ii) diversity sampling suppresses property bias in multi-dimensional regression; (iii) property bias control improves aperiodic designs
- scenario: large shape dataset, no evaluated observations at start
- incrementally "grows" diverse, task-aware dataset (Figure 1)
- (i) compact shape descriptor via unsupervised representation learning; (ii) sparse regressor as start-up "agent"; (iii) curate samples from predictions; batch sequential sampling on shape diversity, estimated property diversity, user-defined quality
- from massive library of building blocks; tailor distribution by diversity and quality

6. Contributions etc.
- principled framework from no evaluated designs; rigorous metrics, little heuristics
- solution to property bias in existing and new datasets
- task-aware datasets tailored to user-defined tasks, keeping shape and property diversity
- advantages: scalability, modularity, customizability, no restriction on shape generation, no domain knowledge needed, applicable to high-dimensional image datasets
- validation: two large-scale shape-only mechanical metamaterial datasets (88,180 and 57,000 instances), different ideas, no preliminary downsampling
- three scenarios: diversity only (general use, e.g. global metamodeling); quality-weighted diversity (task-aware); shape-property joint diversity (tailorable)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Metamaterials are artificially architectured materials that get unusual properties from their structure rather than their composition. Recent advances in computing power and manufacturing have driven research on metamaterials, including theoretical analysis, computational design and experimental validation. In the last two decades outstanding properties and functionalities of metamaterials have been reported in many fields, such as optical, acoustic, thermal, and mechanical. They have been widely used in applications in communications, aerospace, biomedical and defense, among others. From a design point of view, using the rich designability in hierarchical systems is the key to spreading metamaterials further as a versatile material platform, which can realize superior functionalities and also help customization and miniaturization. There is a growing demand for advanced design methods to use the potential of metamaterials.

Data-driven metamaterials design (DDMD) is one way to design metamaterials intelligently. In general the approach has three main steps: data acquisition, model construction, and inference for design. DDMD usually starts with a precomputed dataset with a large number of structure-property pairs. Then a machine learning model is built to learn the mapping from structure to property, and sometimes the other way around. Then the data-driven model is used for design optimization, for example at the "building block" or unit cell level, and optionally also tiling in the macroscale if aperiodic designs are of interest. Compared to conventional approaches, the key differences of DDMD are that (i) DDMD speeds up multiscale design optimization by exploring the vast design space efficiently; (ii) it has few restrictions on analytical formulations of design interest; and (iii) some DDMD approaches allow on-demand design without iterations, which pays off the initial cost of data acquisition and model construction. Because of these advantages, DDMD has reported a lot of achievements for diverse design problems in recent years.

Even though DDMD has surged recently, data acquisition and data quality assessment, which are the very first step of DDMD, have received little attention. In data-driven design data is a design element. A collection of data points forms a landscape that is learned by a model, which is an "abstraction" of the data, and that is explored by model inference or modern optimization methods. So data quality propagates into the later stages. But the downstream impact of naive data acquisition is hard to diagnose and so it is hard to prevent a priori. Underestimating this risk, common practice in DDMD usually uses a large number of space-filling designs in the shape space spanned by the shape parameters. This inevitably leads to imbalance, i.e. distributional bias of data, in the property space formed by the property components. The downstream tasks with a data-driven model, namely training, validation and deployment to design, then mostly happen without rigorous assessment of data quality in terms of diversity, design quality, feasibility and so on. This practice overlooks the data imbalance itself and also its compounding ramification at the design stage, and both of them get in the way of solid deployment of DDMD.

4. METASET (Chan et al.)
- subset selection: small but diverse subsets from fully evaluated database
- evaluate all properties a priori, downsample balanced subset by diversity metrics
- limits: (i) evaluation too expensive for massive (\sim O(10^{4})) database; (ii) diversity alone no customization for tasks

5. t-METASET
- task-aware METASET; starts from sparse observations
- "task-aware": rate points by utility for a specific design scenario, not distributional metrics
- diversity (bias reduction, generic) + quality (particular use) as sampling criteria
- advocate: (i) iterative dataset building; (ii) diversity sampling suppresses property bias in multi-dimensional regression; (iii) property bias control improves aperiodic designs
- scenario: large shape dataset, no evaluated observations at start
- incrementally "grows" diverse, task-aware dataset (Figure 1)
- (i) compact shape descriptor via unsupervised representation learning; (ii) sparse regressor as start-up "agent"; (iii) curate samples from predictions; batch sequential sampling on shape diversity, estimated property diversity, user-defined quality
- from massive library of building blocks; tailor distribution by diversity and quality

6. Contributions etc.
- principled framework from no evaluated designs; rigorous metrics, little heuristics
- solution to property bias in existing and new datasets
- task-aware datasets tailored to user-defined tasks, keeping shape and property diversity
- advantages: scalability, modularity, customizability, no restriction on shape generation, no domain knowledge needed, applicable to high-dimensional image datasets
- validation: two large-scale shape-only mechanical metamaterial datasets (88,180 and 57,000 instances), different ideas, no preliminary downsampling
- three scenarios: diversity only (general use, e.g. global metamodeling); quality-weighted diversity (task-aware); shape-property joint diversity (tailorable)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Metamaterials are artificially architectured materials that get unusual properties from their structure rather than their composition. Recent advances in computing power and manufacturing have driven research on metamaterials, including theoretical analysis, computational design and experimental validation. In the last two decades outstanding properties and functionalities of metamaterials have been reported in many fields, such as optical, acoustic, thermal, and mechanical. They have been widely used in applications in communications, aerospace, biomedical and defense, among others. From a design point of view, using the rich designability in hierarchical systems is the key to spreading metamaterials further as a versatile material platform, which can realize superior functionalities and also help customization and miniaturization. There is a growing demand for advanced design methods to use the potential of metamaterials.

Data-driven metamaterials design (DDMD) is one way to design metamaterials intelligently. In general the approach has three main steps: data acquisition, model construction, and inference for design. DDMD usually starts with a precomputed dataset with a large number of structure-property pairs. Then a machine learning model is built to learn the mapping from structure to property, and sometimes the other way around. Then the data-driven model is used for design optimization, for example at the "building block" or unit cell level, and optionally also tiling in the macroscale if aperiodic designs are of interest. Compared to conventional approaches, the key differences of DDMD are that (i) DDMD speeds up multiscale design optimization by exploring the vast design space efficiently; (ii) it has few restrictions on analytical formulations of design interest; and (iii) some DDMD approaches allow on-demand design without iterations, which pays off the initial cost of data acquisition and model construction. Because of these advantages, DDMD has reported a lot of achievements for diverse design problems in recent years.

Even though DDMD has surged recently, data acquisition and data quality assessment, which are the very first step of DDMD, have received little attention. In data-driven design data is a design element. A collection of data points forms a landscape that is learned by a model, which is an "abstraction" of the data, and that is explored by model inference or modern optimization methods. So data quality propagates into the later stages. But the downstream impact of naive data acquisition is hard to diagnose and so it is hard to prevent a priori. Underestimating this risk, common practice in DDMD usually uses a large number of space-filling designs in the shape space spanned by the shape parameters. This inevitably leads to imbalance, i.e. distributional bias of data, in the property space formed by the property components. The downstream tasks with a data-driven model, namely training, validation and deployment to design, then mostly happen without rigorous assessment of data quality in terms of diversity, design quality, feasibility and so on. This practice overlooks the data imbalance itself and also its compounding ramification at the design stage, and both of them get in the way of solid deployment of DDMD.

Chan et al. presented METASET as a subset selection framework that can find small but diverse subsets from a fully evaluated database. The key idea is to evaluate the properties of all designs a priori and then downsample a balanced subset based on diversity metrics. But the approach is not general enough for data acquisition in DDMD, because (i) design evaluation could be too expensive to build a massive (\sim O(10^{4})) database where all the data is evaluated; (ii) diversity alone does not allow customizing the data for specific design tasks.

To make data acquisition for DDMD more general and efficient, we propose task-aware METASET (t-METASET), paying special attention to starting with sparse observations. Here "task-aware" approaches rate individual data points by their utility for a given specific design scenario, rather than by distributional metrics (e.g., diversity) for general use. The framework handles data bias reduction (for generic use) and design quality (for particular use) at the same time, by using diversity and quality as the sampling criteria, respectively. We advocate that (i) building a good dataset should be an iterative procedure; (ii) diversity sampling can efficiently suppress the property bias of the multi-dimensional regression involved in most DDMD methods; (iii) property bias control significantly improves fully aperiodic metamaterial designs, as recent reports show. Unlike existing work, however, we mainly look for a solution to a common but often overlooked scenario that designers face when preparing data: a large-scale shape dataset has been generated and is about to be observed, without any evaluated observations at the beginning.

Our t-METASET incrementally "grows" a high-quality dataset that is diverse and also task-aware. Figure 1 shows a schematic of the t-METASET procedure. The main ideas are (i) extracting a compact shape descriptor from a shape-only dataset by unsupervised representation learning, (ii) sequentially updating a sparse regressor as a start-up "agent" under sparse observations, and (iii) intelligently curating samples based on the prediction of the regressor, and batch sequential sampling based on shape diversity, estimated property diversity, and user-defined quality. Starting from a massive library of building blocks, the active learning framework steers the data acquisition so that it can tailor the data distribution based on both diversity (for generic use) and quality (for specific use) for given tasks.

In the context of DDMD, t-METASET makes three intellectual contributions:

- Starting without evaluated designs, t-METASET gives a principled framework for building a diverse dataset during data acquisition with rigorous metrics and only a small amount of heuristics;

- The framework gives a solution to the property bias that both existing and newly created metamaterial datasets tend to have;

- t-METASET can produce task-aware datasets whose distributional characteristics can be tailored to user-defined design tasks, while keeping shape and property diversity along the way.

We argue that the advantages of t-METASET are: (i) scalability, (ii) modularity, (iii) customizability to general or specific tasks, (iv) no restrictions on shape generation schemes, (v) no dependency on domain knowledge and, by extension, (vi) applicability to generic design datasets with high-dimensional images. We validate t-METASET on two large-scale shape-only mechanical metamaterial datasets (with 88,180 and 57,000 instances) that are built from different ideas, without preliminary downsampling. The validation has three scenarios with different sampling criteria: (i) only diversity, aiming at general use (e.g., global metamodeling), (ii) quality-weighted diversity aiming at task-aware use, and (iii) shape-property joint diversity for tailorable use.

steps.text:
Metamaterials are artificially architectured materials that support unusual properties from their structure rather than their composition [1]. Recent advances in computing power and manufacturing have fueled research on metamaterials, including theoretical analysis, computational design, and experimental validation. Over the last two decades, outstanding properties and functionalities achievable by metamaterials have been reported in a variety of fields, such as optical [2], acoustic [3], thermal [4], and mechanical [5]. They have been widely deployed in applications in communications, aerospace, biomedical, and defense, to name a few [6]. From a design point of view, leveraging the rich designability in hierarchical systems is key to further disseminating metamaterials as a versatile material platform that not only realizes superior functionalities but also facilitates customization and miniaturization. There has been a growing demand for advanced design methods to harness the potential of metamaterials.

Data-driven metamaterials design (DDMD) offers a route to intelligently design metamaterials. In general, the approach builds on three main steps: data acquisition, model construction, and inference for design purposes. DDMD typically starts with a precomputed dataset that includes a large number of structure-property pairs [7,8,9,10,11]. A machine learning model is then constructed to learn the underlying mapping from structure to property, and sometimes vice versa. The data-driven model is then used for design optimization, such as at the "building block" or unit cell level, and optionally tiling in the macroscale when aperiodic designs are of interest [12,13,14,15]. The key distinctions of DDMD from conventional approaches are that (i) DDMD accelerates multiscale design optimization by exploring the vast design space efficiently; (ii) it has few restrictions on analytical formulations of design interest; and (iii) some DDMD approaches enable on-demand design without iterations, which pays off the initial cost of data acquisition and model construction. Capitalizing on these advantages, DDMD has reported many achievements for diverse design problems in recent years [1,8,9,10,16,17,18].

Despite the recent surge of DDMD, little attention has been given to data acquisition and data quality assessment – the very first step of DDMD. In data-driven design, data is a design element: a collection of data points forms a landscape to be learned by a model, which is an "abstraction" of the data, and to be explored by either model inference or modern optimization methods. Hence data quality propagates into the subsequent stages. Yet the downstream impact of naive data acquisition is opaque to diagnose and thus hard to prevent a priori [19]. Underestimating this risk, common practice in DDMD typically resorts to a large number of space-filling designs in the shape space spanned by the shape parameters. This inevitably creates imbalance – distributional bias of data – in the property space [12,20,11,21] formed by the property components. The downstream tasks involving a data-driven model – training, validation, and deployment to design – mostly follow without rigorous assessment of data quality in terms of diversity, design quality, and feasibility, among others. This practice overlooks not only the data imbalance itself but also its compounding ramification at the design stage, and both impede solid deployment of DDMD.

To this end, Chan et al. presented METASET [11] as a subset selection framework that can identify small yet diverse subsets from a fully evaluated database. The key idea is to evaluate the properties of all the designs a priori, and then downsample a balanced subset based on diversity metrics. Yet the approach lacks generality of data acquisition for DDMD in that: (i) design evaluation could be prohibitively expensive for building a massive (\sim O(10^{4})) database with all the data evaluated; (ii) diversity alone does not offer data customization for specific design tasks.

To enhance the generality and efficiency of data acquisition for DDMD, we propose task-aware METASET (t-METASET), with special attention to starting with sparse observations. Herein, "task-aware" approaches rate individual data points based on their utility for a given specific design scenario, rather than on distributional metrics (e.g., diversity) for general use. The proposed framework handles data bias reduction (for generic use) and design quality (for particular use) simultaneously, by leveraging diversity and quality as the sampling criteria, respectively. We advocate that (i) building a good dataset should be an iterative procedure [22,23]; (ii) diversity sampling [24] can efficiently suppress the property bias of the multi-dimensional regression involved in most DDMD methods [11]; (iii) property bias control significantly improves fully aperiodic metamaterial designs, as shown by recent reports [12,13,14,15]. Distinct from existing work, however, we primarily seek a solution to a common – yet frequently overlooked – scenario that designers face during data preparation: a large-scale shape dataset has been generated and is about to be observed, without evaluated observations at the beginning.

Our t-METASET incrementally "grows" a high-quality dataset that is not only diverse but also task-aware. Figure 1 illustrates a schematic of the t-METASET procedure. The central ideas are (i) to extract a compact shape descriptor from a shape-only dataset by unsupervised representation learning, (ii) to sequentially update a sparse regressor as a start-up "agent" under sparse observations, and (iii) to intelligently curate samples based on the prediction of the regressor, with batch sequential sampling [24] building on shape diversity, estimated property diversity, and user-defined quality. Starting from a massive library of building blocks, the active learning framework maneuvers the data acquisition so that it can tailor the data distribution based on both diversity (for generic use) and quality (for specific use) for given tasks.

In the context of DDMD, the intellectual contributions of t-METASET are three-fold:

- Starting without evaluated designs, t-METASET offers a principled framework for building a diverse dataset during data acquisition with rigorous metrics and a small amount of heuristics;

- The framework provides a solution to the property bias that both existing and newly created metamaterial datasets are prone to;

- The proposed t-METASET can produce task-aware datasets whose distributional characteristics can be tailored in response to user-defined design tasks, while securing shape and property diversity along the way.

We argue that the advantages of t-METASET are: (i) scalability, (ii) modularity, (iii) customizability to general or specific tasks, (iv) freedom from restrictions on shape generation schemes, (v) no dependency on domain knowledge and, by extension, (vi) applicability to generic design datasets involving high-dimensional images. t-METASET is validated on two large-scale shape-only mechanical metamaterial datasets (containing 88,180 and 57,000 instances, respectively) that are built from different ideas, without preliminary downsampling. The validation involves three scenarios addressed by different sampling criteria: (i) only diversity, aiming at general use (e.g., global metamodeling [25,26]), (ii) quality-weighted diversity aiming at task-aware use, and (iii) shape-property joint diversity for tailorable use.
